[[Jacinda Ardern]] | predecessor1 = [[David Cunliffe]]{{efn|[[David Parker (New Zealand politician)|David Parker]] acted from 30 September to 18 November 2014.}} | successor1 = [[Jacinda Ardern]] | office13 = 33rd [[President of the New Zealand Labour Party|President of the Labour Party]] | term_start13 = 2 March 2009 | term_end13 = 2 April 2011 | vice_president13 = [[Moira Coatsworth]] | predecessor13 = [[Mike Williams (New Zealand politician)|Mike Williams]] | successor13 = [[Moira Coatsworth]] | constituency_MP14 = the [[New Zealand Labour Party|Labour]] [[list MP|Party List]] | term_start14 = 26 November 2011 | term_end14 = 5 December 2023 | parliament14 = New Zealand | party = | birth_name = Andrew James Little | birth_date = {{birth date and age|df=y|1965|5|7}} | birth_place = [[New Plymouth]], New Zealand | death_date = | death_place = | spouse = {{marriage|Leigh Fitzgerald|2008}} | children = 1 | education = [[Victoria University of Wellington]] | website = {{URL|https://www.andrewlittle.nz|www.andrewlittle.nz}} }} '''Andrew James Little''' (born 7 May 1965) is a New Zealand politician serving as [[mayor of Wellington]], the [[Capital of New Zealand|capital city of New Zealand]], since 17 October 2025. A lawyer and former trade union official, Little was [[Leader of the New Zealand Labour Party|Leader]] of the [[New Zealand Labour Party|Labour Party]] and [[Leader of the Opposition (New Zealand)|Leader of the Opposition]] from 2014 to 2017 and a senior minister in the [[Sixth Labour Government of New Zealand|Labour governments]] led by [[Jacinda Ardern]] and [[Chris Hipkins]] from 2017 to 2023. Little was first elected as a Labour Party [[list MP]] in 2011, after serving as [[President of the New Zealand Labour Party|President of the Labour Party]] between 2009 and 2011. His political career followed a career in unionism, which included 11 years as the national secretary of the [[Engineering, Printing and Manufacturing Union]], New Zealand's largest private-sector union. Little's term as Labour leader was characterised by low opinion polling results and punctuated by his resignation from the role less than two months before he was due to lead the party in the 2017 general election. Little's decision was described as "selfless" and instrumental in Labour's success under new leader Jacinda Ardern. In the following six years he served as a senior minister and was regarded as a "safe pair of hands" across 12 ministerial portfolios,{{Cite web |date=31 January 2023 |title=PM's chance to carve a new path with Cabinet reshuffle |url=https://www.newsroom.co.nz/page/pms-chance-to-carve-a-new-path-with-cabinet-reshuffle |access-date=17 October 2023 |website=Newsroom |language=en-AU |archive-date=31 January 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230131024833/https://www.newsroom.co.nz/page/pms-chance-to-carve-a-new-path-with-cabinet-reshuffle |url-status=live }} including [[Minister for Treaty of Waitangi Negotiations]], [[Minister of Justice (New Zealand)|Minister of Justice]], [[Minister of Health (New Zealand)|Minister of Health]] and [[Minister of Defence (New Zealand)|Minister of Defence]]. Following the Labour Government's defeat in the [[2023 New Zealand general election|2023 election]], Little declined to return to Parliament as a list MP and returned to legal practice. He resumed his political career in 2025, winning the [[2025 Wellington mayoral election]]. ==Early life== Born in [[New Plymouth]] on 7 May 1965,{{cite web | url=http://www.parliament.nz/en-NZ/MPP/MPs/MPs/3/7/6/50MP175491-Little-Andrew.htm | title=Andrew Little | publisher=[[New Zealand Parliament]] | date=6 March 2013 | access-date=15 February 2015 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130306085725/http://www.parliament.nz/en-NZ/MPP/MPs/MPs/3/7/6/50MP175491-Little-Andrew.htm | archive-date=6 March 2013}} Little was educated at [[New Plymouth Boys' High School]]. His father was a devout [[New Zealand National Party|National Party]] supporter and Little recalls delivering National pamphlets under his father's direction when he was younger.{{Cite news|title = Audrey Young: Little smashed it – literally|url = http://www.nzherald.co.nz/opinion/news/article.cfm?c_id=466&objectid=11542022|work =[[The New Zealand Herald]] |date = 8 November 2015|access-date = 8 November 2015|issn = 1170-0777|last = Young|first = Audrey|archive-date = 23 May 2019|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20190523025803/https://www.nzherald.co.nz/opinion/news/article.cfm?c_id=466&objectid=11542022|url-status = live}} When he was 17, Little got his first job as a labourer digging the main cable trench for a new methanol plant in [[Waitara, New Zealand|Waitara Valley]] as part of the "[[Think Big]]" programme. During his time there he noticed that the contractor he was working for was deliberately using a less than adequate amount of concrete than the work required. He finished work there at the beginning of 1984 and left upon being accepted to enter university.{{Cite news|title = My Summer Job: Andrew Little, Labour Party Leader|url = http://www.nzherald.co.nz/politics/news/article.cfm?c_id=280&objectid=11769617|work = [[The New Zealand Herald]]|date = 4 January 2017|access-date = 4 January 2017|archive-date = 4 January 2017|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20170104083125/http://www.nzherald.co.nz/politics/news/article.cfm?c_id=280&objectid=11769617|url-status = live}} He had also worked as a timber yard worker and in security.{{cite news |last1=Sowman-Lund |first1=Stewart |title=What jobs did our MPs do before they were in parliament? |url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/300829763/what-jobs-did-our-mps-do-before-they-were-in-parliament |access-date=14 March 2023 |work=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] |date=14 March 2023 |language=en |archive-date=14 March 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230314022514/https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/300829763/what-jobs-did-our-mps-do-before-they-were-in-parliament |url-status=live }} In the 1980s Little studied law, philosophy and [[public policy]] at [[Victoria University of Wellington]], where he became active in the campaign against New Zealand's [[student loan]] scheme. He was president of the [[Victoria University of Wellington Students' Association]] for the 1987 academic year and served as [[New Zealand Union of Students' Associations]] (NZUSA) president in 1988 and 1989.{{cite web | url=http://www.students.org.nz/history | title=New Zealand Union of Students' Associations – General History | publisher=NZUSA | access-date=15 February 2015 | archive-date=6 February 2021 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210206053204/https://www.students.org.nz/history | url-status=live }} ==Career with trade unions== After graduating Little took a job as a lawyer with the Engineers' Union (a forerunner of the [[Engineering, Printing and Manufacturing Union|EPMU]]), with his work including [[Accident Compensation Corporation]] (ACC) and [[employment law]] issues.{{cite news | url=http://www.nzherald.co.nz/politics/news/article.cfm?c_id=280&objectid=11339881 | title=Who is Andrew Little? Union chief, lawyer and Gangnam Style dancer | work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] | date=9 October 2014 | access-date=9 October 2014 | last=Davison | first=Isaac | archive-date=10 October 2014 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141010023106/http://www.nzherald.co.nz/politics/news/article.cfm?c_id=280&objectid=11339881 | url-status=live }} In 1997 he was appointed the union's [[general counsel]]. Two years later, he was appointed assistant national secretary, and was elected national secretary when [[Rex Jones]] stood down from the position in 2000.{{cite web|url=http://www.radionz.co.nz/news/political/259657/little-takes-union-path-to-leadership|access-date=26 September 2017|title=Little takes union path to leadership|date=18 November 2014|publisher=Radio NZ – radionz.co.nz|archive-date=27 September 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170927000009/http://www.radionz.co.nz/news/political/259657/little-takes-union-path-to-leadership|url-status=live}} In 2007 Little was ranked at number 40 on the [[New Zealand Listener Power List]].{{cite news | url=http://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=10463577 | title=Clark still most powerful but Key nipping at her heels | work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] | date=14 September 2007 | agency=NZPA | access-date=15 February 2015}} Little became an important extra-parliamentary figure within the Labour Party and was one of the main advisors from the trade unions. Political commentators quickly identified him as a potential future Labour Party leader and prime minister.{{cite web |last=Johnston |first=Kirsty |date=20 July 2010 |title=Andrew Little to run for Parliament |url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/3936152/Andrew-Little-to-run-for-Parliament |access-date=31 December 2025 |website=Stuff}} In his first term, he held the [[Accident Compensation Corporation|ACC]] shadow portfolio and gained profile during the National-led government's restructuring of the organisation. Together with [[Trevor Mallard]], he launched attacks against ACC Minister [[Judith Collins]], who eventually responded with issuing a defamation claim in May 2012. At the time, Little stated the bill was needed because "the track record of prosecutions under the [[Health and Safety at Work Act 2015|Health and Safety Act]] is that they tend to focus on lower level failures because getting the evidence and securing the conviction are easier, but personal responsibility for fatalities goes unchecked."{{cite news | url=http://www.3news.co.nz/politics/corporate-manslaughter-charge-in-new-bill-2012111511 |title=Corporate manslaughter charge in new bill|date=15 November 2012 | publisher=3News | access-date=19 March 2015}} A 2012 ''[[3News]]'' poll found that seventy-four percent of respondents would like to see a charge of corporate manslaughter introduced.{{cite news | url=http://www.3news.co.nz/politics/government-looking-at-corporate-manslaughter-laws-2012120619 |title=Government looking at corporate manslaughter laws|date=6 December 2012 | publisher=3News | access-date=19 March 2015}} The Bill was eventually transferred to the name of [[David Cunliffe]] but was not drawn before Cunliffe's retirement from Parliament in early 2017.{{Cite web|title=Members' bills ballot for Thursday, 1 December 2016 – New Zealand Parliament|url=https://www.parliament.nz/en/pb/bills-and-laws/members-bills-ballots-archive/document/51HOOOCBallot201612011/members-bills-ballot-for-thursday-1-december-2016|access-date=10 February 2022|website=www.parliament.nz|language=en|archive-date=10 February 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220210005427/https://www.parliament.nz/en/pb/bills-and-laws/members-bills-ballots-archive/document/51HOOOCBallot201612011/members-bills-ballot-for-thursday-1-december-2016|url-status=dead}} ===Second term and leadership (2014–2017)=== [[File:Andrew Little gives State of the Nation speech 06.JPG|thumb|left|Little's 'State of the Nation' speech, January 2016]] At the [[2014 New Zealand general election|2014 election]] he again stood and lost in the New Plymouth electorate. A reluctant assessment|url=https://www.nbr.co.nz/opinion/can-andrew-little-win-next-year-election-labour-reluctant-assessment-be|website=The National Business Review|access-date=15 November 2016|date=1 July 2016|archive-date=16 November 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161116061749/https://www.nbr.co.nz/opinion/can-andrew-little-win-next-year-election-labour-reluctant-assessment-be|url-status=dead}} The election used an [[electoral college]] system where unions affiliated to the Labour Party had 20 percent of the vote; while Robertson had led Little in the caucus and party membership sections, the unions' support contributed to Little's narrow victory.{{cite news |last1=Watkins |first1=Tracy |last2=Fox |first2=Michael |last3=Vance |first3=Andrea |date=18 November 2014 |title=Little wins Labour leadership |url=http://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/9166765/Little-wins-Labour-leadership |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240930001138/https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/9166765/Little-wins-Labour-leadership |archive-date=30 September 2024 |access-date=18 November 2014 |work=[[Stuff.co.nz]]}} As Leader of the Labour Party and [[Leader of the Opposition (New Zealand)|Leader of the Opposition]], Little sought to challenge the Government with a strong alternative narrative. In a 2015 conference speech he introduced a new "Kiwi dream" theme (the [[New Zealand dream]]). In 2015 Labour introduced a new slogan, "Backing the Kiwi Dream".{{cite web|title=Little: Backing The Kiwi Dream – It's Our Future|url=https://itsourfuture.org.nz/little-backing-the-kiwi-dream/|website=It's Our Future|access-date=15 November 2016|date=1 February 2016|archive-date=16 November 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161116020728/https://itsourfuture.org.nz/little-backing-the-kiwi-dream/|url-status=live}} Little largely focused on issues and concerns such as rising house prices in urban areas, a '[[brain drain]]', unemployment and [[job security]] and the growing wage gap between [[baby boomers]] and [[millennials]]. The "Kiwi dream" narrative was particularly designed to engage young voters.{{cite web|title=Labour will not abandon our young people as National has Labour will|url=https://socialfeed.info/labour-will-not-abandon-our-young-people-as-national-has-labour-will-9019482|website=socialfeed.info|access-date=15 November 2016|archive-date=16 November 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161116015952/https://socialfeed.info/labour-will-not-abandon-our-young-people-as-national-has-labour-will-9019482|url-status=usurped}} Little appointed long-serving Labour MP [[Annette King]] as Labour's 'interim' deputy leader shortly after his election as leader. Little was elected as a Cabinet Minister by the Labour Party caucus following Labour's [[Sixth Labour Government of New Zealand|formation of a government]] with [[New Zealand First]] and the [[Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand|Greens]]. In late October 2017, Little assumed several portfolios including [[Minister of Justice (New Zealand)|Minister of Justice]], [[Minister for Courts]], Minister Responsible for the [[Government Communications Security Bureau]] (GCSB) and the [[New Zealand Security Intelligence Service]] (NZSIS), Minister for [[Treaty of Waitangi]] Negotiations, and Minister Responsible for [[Pike River Recovery Agency|Pike River Re-entry]].{{cite web |date=26 October 2017 |title=Ministerial List |url=http://www.dpmc.govt.nz/cabinet/ministers/ministerial-list |publisher=DPMC |access-date=26 October 2017 |archive-date=11 June 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170611144919/http://www.dpmc.govt.nz/cabinet/ministers/ministerial-list |url-status=live }} Following the success of the pilot [[Alcohol and Other Drug Treatment Court]] (the AODTC) at reducing reoffending, in December 2017, Little announced that alcohol and drug courts would be rolled out nationwide.[https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/crime/100100936/government-to-roll-out-specialised-drug-and-alcohol-courts-from-2018 Government to roll out specialised drug and alcohol courts from 2018] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230708064252/https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/crime/100100936/government-to-roll-out-specialised-drug-and-alcohol-courts-from-2018 |date=8 July 2023 }}, Stuff, 24 December 2017 Two years later, he said the AODTC had proved effective, reducing reoffending by 23% up to two years after treatment.Government makes drug court permanent in justice shake-up, NZ Herald, 12 December 2019. |date=11 October 2025 |access-date=11 October 2025 }} == Wellington mayoralty (2025–present) == {{See also|2025 Wellington mayoral election}} In late October 2025, Little appointed Labour councillor [[Ben McNulty]] as deputy mayor.{{Cite web |last=James |first=Nick |date=29 October 2025 |title=Ben McNulty named as Wellington's new deputy mayor |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/national/577175/ben-mcnulty-named-as-wellington-s-new-deputy-mayor |website=[[Radio New Zealand]]}} In November 2025, Little promoted independent conservative councillor Diane Calvert as chair of the [[Wellington City Council]]'s budget committee and independent conservative councillor [[Ray Chung]] as chair of the council-controlled organisations committee. The four [[Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand|Green]]-aligned councillors criticised Chung's nomination due to his smear campaign against the previous Mayor [[Tory Whanau]] but agreed to support Little's nominations in the "interests of being constructive partners."{{cite news |last1=McNamus |first1=Joel |title=Andrew Little buddies up to the right |url=https://thespinoff.co.nz/politics/25-11-2025/andrew-little-buddies-up-to-the-right |access-date=29 November 2025 |work=[[The Spinoff]] |date=25 November 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251129194955/https://thespinoff.co.nz/politics/25-11-2025/andrew-little-buddies-up-to-the-right |archive-date=29 November 2025}} In late November 2025, Little and the Labour-aligned councillors supported reviewing the contentious Golden Mile pedestrianisation project for three-to-six months. The Green-aligned councillors and [[iwi]] representatives Holden Hohaia and Liz Kelly opposed farther delays to the Golden Mile project, which the Council had begun planning in 2021. The motion to implement a three-to-six months review of the Golden Mile project passed by a margin of 12 to 4 votes; with Little, the Labour councillors and the independents supporting the motion and the Green councillors opposing it. In February 2026, Little called for an independent inquiry into the failure of Wellington's [[Moa Point]] sewage plant.{{Cite news |date=9 February 2026 |title=Wellington mayor Andrew Little wants ministerial inquiry into Moa Point sewage plant failure |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/top/586333/wellington-mayor-andrew-little-wants-ministerial-inquiry-into-moa-point-sewage-plant-failure |work=RNZ}}{{Cite news |last=Gibbens |first=Krystal |date=6 February 2026 |title=Wellington Mayor Andrew Little says he will bring 'catastrophic' sewage failure to PM's attention |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/national/586113/wellington-mayor-andrew-little-says-he-will-bring-catastrophic-sewage-failure-to-pm-s-attention |work=RNZ}} On 8 June 2026, Little declared a state of emergency in [[Wellington]]'s southern and eastern wards in response to heavy swells. Residents of [[Owhiro Bay]], [[Island Bay]], [[Houghton Bay]] and [[Breaker Bay]] were ordered to evacuate by 9am on 9 June.{{Cite news |last1=Nightingale |first1=Melissa |date=8 June 2026 |title=Emergency evacuation order issued for parts of Wellington over 'significant swells event' |url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/wellington/significant-swell-event-metservice-warns-of-possible-8-10m-waves-in-wellington-wairarapa/B3PNH5RRWFHPVFJUVBKGC4RFZU/ |access-date=8 June 2026 |work=[[The New Zealand Herald]]}} On 18 June, Little as Mayor joined the majority of the Wellington City Council in voting to discontinue work on the $139 million [[Golden Mile, Wellington|Golden Mile]] pedestrianisation project.
